Share on X Telegram Nigeria’s Ministry of Steel Development is on the path of bureaucratic redundancy: an institution whose industrial ambitions remain disconnected from the country’s manufacturing reality.
Since 1999, successive governments have promised to transform Nigeria into a steel-producing nation. Under Olusegun Obasanjo, Olu Agunloye served as minister of power and steel, followed by Olusegun Agagu.
Subsequent administrations brought ministers including Sarafa Ishola, Diezani Alison-Madueke, Musa Sada, Kayode Fayemi, Abubakar Bawa Bwari, Olamilekan Adegbite, and, since 2023, Shuaibu Audu. Yet Ajaokuta Steel Company remains the enduring symbol of industrial failure.
Audu can point to investment promotion, a commissioned steel-processing facility, and agreements aimed at reviving dormant industrial assets.
But these achievements should not be equated with rebuilding Nigeria’s integrated steel industry.
The problem transcends individual ministers. Abandoned projects, inadequate infrastructure, unreliable electricity, and governance failures have undermined successive revival efforts.
Billions have been discussed, investors have been courted, and technical assessments have been commissioned, but Nigeria still struggles to translate its iron ore deposits into competitive domestic steel production.
Aliko Dangote briefly offered hope in 2024, announcing plans to enter steel production and supply West Africa.
Two months later, he abandoned the proposal, citing concerns that his investment would attract accusations of monopoly, preferring instead to invest in power generation.
It was a curious choice, considering that he has invested in a vehicle assembly plant and needs earth-moving equipment more than any other industrialist.
Nevertheless, his withdrawal exposed a troubling investment climate in which even ambitious domestic capital may hesitate to pursue strategic industrial projects.
Egypt’s established steelmakers and vehicle-assembly operations demonstrate how domestic production can support industrial value chains, although neither country manufactures everything it consumes.
Steel alone does not manufacture cars, ships, or weapons. Skilled engineers, reliable energy, technology, financing, and sustained industrial policy are equally essential.
Nevertheless, without competitively priced steel, Nigeria’s ambitions in shipbuilding, vehicle manufacturing, construction, and defence production incur additional costs and become more dependent on imports.
Audu and the ministry he heads can only be measured by outcomes, not announcements.
Can he restore viable production, attract credible investors, and establish transparent, time-bound targets?
Until Nigerians see steel plants operating competitively, the ministry will remain vulnerable to an uncomfortable question: what, precisely, has it delivered for industrialisation?
